item.title: Ep 8 – Best of the week: the founder, the float and the phone (14 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Best of the week: Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia, Anthropic sets its IPO range, models get cheaper, agents formalise Fermat and verify Signal, and security stays the weak spot. Plus one story we missed, OpenAI folding its robotics team into main research, and the top three agent projects of the week: Pinky, REA and Uber's ADR.

The week in review

  • Nvidia: NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition (Colette Kress interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones first chair), after the board's investigation covered in Ep 4. Coverage: TechCrunch, AP.
  • Anthropic: roadshow launch, $70–$78 a share, Nasdaq "ANT", pricing expected 18 Nov; TechCrunch on the $1.404T fully diluted valuation. Compare OpenAI's $11B raise at $1.25T (Ep 3).
  • Cheaper models: Meta Muse Ember (Ep 4), Gemini 4 Carbon now available (Ep 6), Amazon replaces Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider (Ep 5).
  • Proofs: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 formalise Fermat's Last Theorem with 1,000 agents in 30 hours (Ep 4); Introducing AlphaProof Code verifies Signal's implementation (Ep 5).
  • Security: Apiiro on Claude Code's "don't ask again" secrets (1,122 public GitHub files, Ep 3); Fireworks AI incident update and Notion's notice (Ep 5); VulnCheck on Glasswing (Ep 6).
  • Missed this week: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots (Fortune, 13 Nov): robotics research moves to main research under Mark Chen, applied robotics and hardware to Applied under Greg Brockman; an Astra-powered agent scored 74.8% on a simulated manipulation benchmark in an Nvidia study vs 51.0% for the best specialised models; OpenAI's CoRL booth #208 sat empty. HN discussion.

Top 3 agent projects of the week

  • Pinky (DIYgod, Apache-2.0): lets any MCP agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more) operate a real iPhone or Android phone while you watch, approve risky steps or take over; approvals (payments by default, optionally messages) are enforced by Pinky's gateway, not by instructions to the agent; native app, no Electron.
  • REA: Reverse Engineer Anything (morluto, MIT; rea.tools): one MCP server for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript/Electron apps, .NET assemblies and websites without source; can drive Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna; runs locally and reports the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion.
  • ADR: Agentic AI Detection and Response (Uber, Apache-2.0): deployed in production at Uber; discovers AI tools and MCP servers on endpoints, traces agent activity across 7+ AI coding tools, ADR-Bench with 300+ tasks, 134 MCP servers and all 17 agent attack techniques, and a two-tier detector; paper accepted to MLSys 2026.

Recommended

  • The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development (Dwarkesh Patel, 13 Nov 2026; also narrated on his podcast): his median for automated researchers matching the best human AI researchers is 2028, citing AI progress in math, including the Claude Fermat formalisation. HN discussion.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Dreamy Flashback”, “Lobby Time”, “Enchanted Valley” by Kevin MacLeod (CC BY 4.0); “More On That Later”, “What's Behind the Door”, “Something To Fill The Space” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via incompetech.com / Free Music Archive / OpenGameArt; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “85 Short music jingles” by Kenney (CC0 1.0); “202 More Sound Effects” by OwlishMedia (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: On Tuesday's show, Nvidia's board was investigating its founder.

B: By Friday's, he was gone. And that wasn't even the only trillion-dollar story of the week.

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Saturday the fourteenth of November, so it's the best of the week, then three agent projects worth your weekend.

* * *

A: Start with the money. Jensen Huang resigned on Wednesday, and CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, with Harvey Jones as the board's first-ever chair.

B: The same week Anthropic opened its IPO roadshow. Seventy to seventy-eight dollars a share, ticker A-N-T, up to about one point four trillion dollars.

A: Which edges past OpenAI's one point two five trillion from Monday's show. Pricing is due on Wednesday.

B: Meanwhile the models got cheaper. Meta's Muse Ember, Gemini 4 Carbon at an introductory price, and Amazon swapping Sonnet for a one-token decision model at ninety-eight percent less.

A: Then the proofs. A thousand Claude agents formalised Fermat's Last Theorem in thirty hours, and DeepMind's AlphaProof Code verified Signal's implementation, down to the compiled code.

B: But security kept up the counterweight. Claude Code's "don't ask again" settings leaked secrets into more than eleven hundred public files, and the Fireworks breach reached Notion AI chats.

A: So the week in one line: agents got good at checkable work, and the infrastructure around them stayed the weak spot.

* * *

B: One we missed. Fortune reported on Friday that OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team.

A: The researchers move into main research under Mark Chen. The bet is that general models like GPT-6 Astra can drive robots directly.

B: In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent hit seventy-four point eight percent on a simulated manipulation benchmark, against fifty-one for the best specialised models.

A: And OpenAI's booth at the CoRL robotics conference this week? It sat empty.

* * *

B: Now the builds. Three projects, one pattern: agents getting hands, with someone holding the leash.

A: First, Pinky. Any MCP agent, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, can operate a real iPhone or Android phone while you watch from your computer.

B: And the clever bit is where the safety lives. Approvals for payments or messages are enforced by Pinky's gateway, not by asking the agent nicely.

A: Right, the tap waits until you allow it.

B: Second, REA, short for Reverse Engineer Anything. One MCP server that lets your agent inspect native binaries, Electron apps, dotnet assemblies and websites, without source code.

A: It drives tools you may already have, like Ghidra, IDA or Hopper, runs locally, and attaches the evidence and limitations behind every conclusion.

B: See a feature in someone's app, and the agent explains it and builds your version.

* * *

A: And third, the one that watches the other two. Uber's ADR, Agentic AI Detection and Response.

B: It's running in production at Uber. It finds the AI tools on employee machines, MCP servers included, and traces what coding agents actually do across seven-plus tools.

A: Plus ADR-Bench: more than three hundred tasks, a hundred and thirty-four MCP servers, all seventeen agent attack techniques. The paper was accepted at MLSys.

B: Phone, binary, and the security team's view of both. Same week, same lesson as the Claude Code leak.

A: One recommendation for the weekend: Dwarkesh Patel's new essay, "The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development". He now puts his median for AI matching the best AI researchers at twenty twenty-eight.

B: He even uses this week's Fermat formalisation as his example. Links to everything are in the notes. See you Monday.

item.title: Ep 7 – The founder leaves (13 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO and Colette Kress steps in as interim chief; Anthropic launches its IPO roadshow at up to a $1.4 trillion valuation; and AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS for coding agents, written and tested entirely by agents.

  • NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition (Nvidia, 12 Nov) and the SEC 8-K filing: board accepted Huang's resignation as President, CEO and director on 11 Nov, effective immediately; CFO Colette Kress (CFO since 2013) is interim CEO and stays CFO; Harvey C. Jones, on the board since 1993, appointed first-ever chair. Coverage: TechCrunch (shares down nearly 12% in early trading; more than $855B of market cap lost since Friday; $99B of investments plus $25B of commitments; CoreWeave down about 9%; about 60 direct reports and no succession plan; earnings next Tuesday), AP, The New York Times on the second relationship. HN discussion.
  • Callback: Ep 4 (10 Nov) covered the Nvidia board's independent investigation into Huang's relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang.
  • Anthropic launches roadshow for proposed IPO (Anthropic, 10 Nov) and the IPO site: 825M Class A shares at $70–$78 on Nasdaq as "ANT"; pricing expected 18 Nov, trading 19 Nov (EST); Q3 2026 revenue $17.0B, more than 12x year on year. Coverage: TechCrunch (up to $64.35B raised, $1.404T fully diluted at the top; $26B Class N private sale to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC, with Google and Nvidia at $10B each; nine-month net loss of $104B), CNBC (about 20% retail allocation; a $2T valuation was earlier in view), Quartz (WSJ: large backers pressed for a lower number after the AI sell-off). HN discussion.
  • Callback: Ep 3 (9 Nov) covered OpenAI raising $11B at a $1.25T valuation.
  • AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code (Swami Sivasubramanian, guest post on Werner Vogels' All Things Distributed, 11 Nov): a local, offline AWS for coding agents to test against; all code written and tested by agents from 400+ Smithy API models covering 200+ services, using fidelity tests verified against real AWS; first SQS version from one Kiro prompt in about 15 minutes; merge gate with several adversarial security agents; CC0 licence; a "things-that-do-not-work" folder lists known gaps; rebuilding the Alf replication engine took four nights going nowhere until the agent had a spec and test environment, then about two hours ("it had no way to check its results"). Code: aws/aws-emulator. HN discussion.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Cloudloop”, “Glass Android”, “Under Suspicion”, “Bigger Questions”, “Credit Roll” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0); “Discovery Hit”, “Easy Lemon” by Kevin MacLeod (CC BY 4.0); “WWS Cashregister” by Work With Sounds / Werstas (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive / OpenGameArt / incompetech.com / Wikimedia Commons; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “85 Short music jingles” by Kenney (CC0 1.0); [“Keyboard Soundpack #1 [Typing and Single Keystrokes]”](https://opengameart.org/content/keyboard-soundpack-1-typing-and-single-keystrokes) by unicaegames (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

B: In nineteen ninety-three, Jensen Huang co-founded a graphics chip company and became its CEO.

A: Thirty-three years later, he has resigned. Effective immediately.

* * *

B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

A: And I'm William. It's Friday the thirteenth of November.

B: Today: Nvidia without its founder, Anthropic's price tag for Wall Street, and a copy of AWS written entirely by agents.

* * *

A: On Tuesday's show, Nvidia's board had just opened an investigation into Huang's relationship with an executive U.S. officials link to Chinese intelligence.

B: Then late Wednesday the New York Times reported a second relationship, with an Nvidia employee who reports to him.

A: By Thursday he was gone. President, CEO and board member, all at once.

B: The interim CEO is Colette Kress, the CFO since twenty thirteen. She keeps the CFO job too.

A: And the board gets its first-ever chair: Harvey Jones, who has sat on it since nineteen ninety-three.

B: The stock fell nearly twelve percent in early trading. TechCrunch counts more than eight hundred and fifty billion dollars of value gone since last Friday.

A: And it reaches well beyond Nvidia: ninety-nine billion dollars of investments, in OpenAI, Anthropic, CoreWeave and more. CoreWeave fell nine percent the same day.

B: And Huang ran it with about sixty direct reports and no named heir.

A: First test of the new Nvidia: earnings, next Tuesday.

* * *

B: One of those Nvidia bets is about to go public. Anthropic has started its roadshow.

A: Eight hundred and twenty-five million shares at seventy to seventy-eight dollars each, on Nasdaq under the ticker A-N-T.

B: At the top of the range that's about sixty-four billion dollars raised, and a fully diluted valuation of one point four trillion.

A: Just above OpenAI, which on Monday's show raised at one point two five trillion.

B: But short of the two trillion floated a few months ago. The Wall Street Journal says big backers pushed it down after last week's AI sell-off.

A: Behind it: seventeen billion dollars of third-quarter revenue, more than twelve times a year earlier.

B: And a nine-month net loss of a hundred and four billion, mostly a non-cash charge because its own valuation went up.

A: Plus a twenty-six billion private sale on the side, to chipmakers and clouds including Google, Microsoft, TSMC, and yes, Nvidia, ten billion of it.

B: So the companies selling Anthropic its compute are also buying its stock.

A: Exactly. Pricing is set for November eighteenth, trading the day after, with about a fifth of the shares aimed at retail investors.

* * *

B: Twenty years ago, Swami Sivasubramanian spent four months building a replication engine for the lock service underneath S3 and DynamoDB.

A: Recently he asked Kiro, Amazon's coding agent, to rebuild it. Four nights of supervising, going nowhere.

B: Then he saw the problem. In his words, the agent "had no way to check its results." Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

A: That lesson is now a product. AWS Emulator is a local, offline copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. Free, and released into the public domain.

B: And it was written entirely by agents. They start from AWS's public API models, write tests, correct them until they pass against real AWS, then build the emulator until it passes the same tests.

A: More than two hundred services. It began with a single prompt for SQS, and a first version came back in about fifteen minutes.

B: Every change passes a merge gate where security agents attack it. And the repo keeps a folder called things-that-do-not-work.

A: So the real story here is the job description. Swami says the engineer now builds the specs, tests and gates that decide when the agents' work is correct.

B: That's Almost Human 365 for Friday. Links are in the episode notes, and tomorrow, the best of the week.

  • Gemini 4 Carbon is now available (Google, 10 Nov): API for all paying developers, rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Antigravity, the Gemini app and AI Mode; built for long-horizon, multi-step coding and research, using more tokens than Argon; #1 on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR and Zapier's AutomationBench at more than 2x lower cost per task than the next best external model (Google's figures); introductory price $2 / $10 per million input / output tokens, rising to $4 / $20 after 30 Nov 2026; /swarm preview in Antigravity; pelican-on-a-GBike campus game demo; 100% recall on scanning in Project Fortify on an internal benchmark. HN discussion.
  • Callback: Ep 5's AlphaProof Code verification of the Signal implementation, which used Gemini Carbon agents.

HN discussion.

A: October the eighteenth. A software engineer travelling in Peru wonders what the explorer who found Machu Picchu would have done with today's tools.

B: That night he points forty-eight AI agents at NASA lidar of the Maya region in Mexico, and goes to bed.

A: By morning, they've found a pyramid that, apparently, nobody had ever mapped.

* * *

B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

A: And I'm William. It's Thursday the twelfth of November.

B: Today: a pyramid that wasn't new, Google's strongest model goes public, and a mountain of AI bug reports nobody can get through.

A: The engineer is Pietro Miotti. His agents turned about twelve hundred square kilometres of lidar into images.

B: And no special classifier. Each agent literally looked at the pictures, with a written guide: pyramids, platforms and plazas in; hills, sinkholes and roads out.

A: One hilltop stood out. A levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least eight to twelve metres tall, and a hollow that may have held rainwater.

B: So he asked the agents to search the literature and the archives. Their answer: not registered.

A: He sent a report to INAH, Mexico's national heritage institute. Three days after the first idea, they replied: no registered site at that location.

B: He wrote, "This is by far the best time ever to be alive." And the post shot up Hacker News.

* * *

A: Then the archaeologists read it.

B: The site was already in a 2025 paper by Francisco Estrada-Belli and colleagues. It just wasn't in INAH's register yet.

A: The agents missed it in the literature search, and his update now says they rediscovered it, not discovered it.

B: So the scan held up. What failed was the step that sounds easiest: checking whether anyone got there first.

A: Yesterday on this show, DeepMind verified Signal's code with agents running Gemini Carbon.

B: And now it's out. Gemini 4 Carbon is in the API for paying developers, and in the Gemini app and Antigravity for Ultra subscribers.

A: Google positions it above Argon, for long, multi-step coding and research. It spends more tokens exploring and verifying.

B: Google says it ranks first on CursorBench four point oh, at under half the cost per task of the next best outside model.

A: And the price matches Argon: two dollars per million input tokens, ten per million output.

B: Until November the thirtieth. Then it doubles, to four and twenty.

A: The new toy is slash swarm in Antigravity. One prompt becomes a team of agents, Carbon on design and auditing, lighter models doing the parallel work.

B: The demo that sells it: a 3D game where you explore Google's campus as a pelican riding a bike.

A: The cyber pitch is louder. In Google's own scanning system, Carbon hit a hundred percent recall on an internal benchmark.

B: But finding bugs was never the hard part.

* * *

A: Seven months ago Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, promising thousands of serious open-source vulnerabilities found by its models.

B: Patrick Garrity at VulnCheck has been keeping score. Anthropic's own ledger, as of November the second: thirty-seven thousand nine hundred and sixty-six findings.

A: Fixed: two hundred and seventeen.

B: In the last two months alone, almost twelve thousand new findings. Fifteen more fixes.

A: And more than sixteen hundred are now marked duplicates, often because someone else found and fixed the bug first.

B: Anthropic named the problem in October. It wrote that it's "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings."

A: Its answer is an OSS Scanner: model-generated reports with no human review, sent to maintainers who opt in.

B: Curl just received forty-five of them. Daniel Stenberg is publishing them slowly, "to soften the impact for the team."

A: Of the first thirty-four, nineteen weren't vulnerabilities at all. Six were confirmed, all low severity.

B: Against a claimed true positive rate of ninety-four percent.

A: The takeaway: in security the scoreboard isn't bugs found, it's bugs fixed. And the fixing still runs on human hours.

B: That's Almost Human 365 for Thursday. Links to everything are in the episode notes, and we're back tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 4 – A thousand agents, thirty hours (10 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 formalise Fermat's Last Theorem with 1,000 agents in 30 hours; Meta's Muse Ember prices a worker model at $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens as companies like Apple ration AI budgets; and Nvidia's board opens an independent investigation after reporting that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

  • Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 (Anthropic, 9 Nov): same underlying model; Fable with cyber/bio safeguards for all users, Mythos via Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs; $8/$40 per million input/output tokens (fast mode $16/$80); FrontierCode 2.0 49.1% at Xhigh vs Opus 5.5 45.5% and GPT-6 Astra 42.8%; first Fermat's Last Theorem formalisation took 11 days with an unreleased research model plus human guidance, 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents did it in 30 hours with a proof 7× shorter, Opus 5.5 reached 26% in 18 hours; 1,000+ subagents over eight days built a bootable prototype OS; training limited gains in accelerator kernel optimisation and LLM architecture research (about Opus 5.5 level there); Fable pitched as Advisor/Orchestrator for smaller models. HN discussion.
  • Counterpoint on machine-checked proofs: OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof called into question (King's College London) and the preprint Navier–Stokes lost in translation (Bastounis, Circelli, Hansen): the Lean formalisation does not correspond to the written proof. Background: OpenAI on Navier–Stokes.
  • Introducing Muse Ember (Meta, 9 Nov): smallest Muse model for tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks; $0.10 input / $0.50 output per million tokens, 1M context, up to 512K output; matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost; FrontierCode 2.0-AA 27.2 vs Haiku 5.5 34.9; Terminal-Bench 4.0 40.9 vs 39.2; AutomationBench-AA 37.8 vs 13.9. HN discussion.
  • Apple cuts internal AI usage budgets (Bloomberg, 4 Nov): some engineers' daily cap cut from $300 to $200, some teams asked to use cheaper models or on-device AI. Summary: MacRumors.
  • Statement from NVIDIA Board of Directors and Jensen Huang's message to staff (Nvidia, 8 Nov). Coverage: The Guardian (NYT reporting on Alice Huang of Megaspeed; Trump: "I think he's an honorable guy"; House Republicans request a closed-door briefing), Reuters explainer via Investing.com (Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner investigated over access to export-barred chips), NPR (China calls the allegations unsubstantiated).

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Evening Glow”, “Tech Toys”, “Curiousity”, “Glass Android”, “Bigger Questions”, “Under Suspicion”, “Credit Roll” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: Thirty hours. A thousand copies of the same model, an empty proof file, and one of the most famous theorems in mathematics. When the clock stopped, Fermat's Last Theorem had been checked by a machine, line by line.

* * *

B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

A: And I'm William. It's Tuesday the tenth of November.

B: Today: Anthropic's new top models, Meta's smallest one at the other end of the price list, and a board investigation at Nvidia.

* * *

A: That run came from Claude Fable 5.2, released by Anthropic alongside Mythos 5.2, the same model without some cyber and biology safeguards, for vetted teams only. Anthropic's first formalisation of Fermat took eleven days, with a human guiding it. A thousand Fable agents did it in thirty hours, with a proof seven times shorter. Opus 5.5, same setup, had about a quarter done at eighteen hours.

B: One caveat carries over from OpenAI's Navier–Stokes claim. In October, mathematicians at King's College London and Cambridge argued that its Lean version didn't match the written proof. A machine check covers exactly the statements it's given, and no more.

A: For developers: forty-nine point one percent on FrontierCode 2.0 at top effort, ahead of Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Price drops to eight dollars per million input tokens and forty output. In one experiment, over a thousand subagents spent eight days building an operating system that boots on a laptop.

B: And one deliberate gap. Anthropic says it limited gains in kernel optimisation and model-architecture research during training, so there Fable sits at roughly Opus 5.5 level.

A: Why this news is important: frontier releases are now measured in agent-days of autonomous work, and labs are openly choosing which capabilities not to ship.

* * *

B: Same day, opposite end. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for the steps agents repeat all day: tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks. Ten cents per million input tokens. Fifty cents output. A million tokens of context.

B: Meta says it matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost.

A: Meta's own table has the counterpoint. On FrontierCode 2.0, which judges whether code would actually get merged, Ember scores twenty-seven point two. Haiku scores thirty-four point nine.

B: Where it leads is volume work, like Terminal-Bench 4.0 and business-workflow automation.

A: The cost pressure behind it is real. Bloomberg reports Apple cut some engineers' daily AI budget from three hundred dollars to two hundred, and is asking some teams to use cheaper models.

B: Why this news is important: the agent stack is splitting into planners and workers. Anthropic itself pitches Fable as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, and those worker models set what an agent fleet costs.

* * *

A: Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation involving its own chief executive. In October, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at the Singapore cloud firm Megaspeed. U.S. officials, the Times says, concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner, and the U.S. has investigated it over suspicions it helped Beijing reach export-barred chips.

A: Over the weekend, Huang admitted the affair in a note to staff. The board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China calls the allegations unsubstantiated.

B: Washington is split. President Trump called Huang "an honorable guy." House Republicans want a closed-door briefing on Nvidia's protections against foreign espionage. Why this news is important: the fight over AI chip exports now runs through the industry's most important CEO, and his access to policymakers is exactly why it matters.

* * *

B: A thousand agents, thirty hours, one very old theorem. Sources are in the notes. See you tomorrow.

  • Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 (Anthropic, 9 Nov): same underlying model; Fable with cyber/bio safeguards for all users, Mythos via Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs; $8/$40 per million input/output tokens (fast mode $16/$80); FrontierCode 2.0 49.1% at Xhigh vs Opus 5.5 45.5% and GPT-6 Astra 42.8%; first Fermat's Last Theorem formalisation took 11 days with an unreleased research model plus human guidance, 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents did it in 30 hours with a proof 7× shorter, Opus 5.5 reached 26% in 18 hours; 1,000+ subagents over eight days built a bootable prototype OS; training limited gains in accelerator kernel optimisation and LLM architecture research (about Opus 5.5 level there); Fable pitched as Advisor/Orchestrator for smaller models. HN discussion.
  • Counterpoint on machine-checked proofs: OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof called into question (King's College London) and the preprint Navier–Stokes lost in translation (Bastounis, Circelli, Hansen): the Lean formalisation does not correspond to the written proof. Background: OpenAI on Navier–Stokes.
  • Introducing Muse Ember (Meta, 9 Nov): smallest Muse model for tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks; $0.10 input / $0.50 output per million tokens, 1M context, up to 512K output; matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost; FrontierCode 2.0-AA 27.2 vs Haiku 5.5 34.9; Terminal-Bench 4.0 40.9 vs 39.2; AutomationBench-AA 37.8 vs 13.9. HN discussion.
  • Apple cuts internal AI usage budgets (Bloomberg, 4 Nov): some engineers' daily cap cut from $300 to $200, some teams asked to use cheaper models or on-device AI. Summary: MacRumors.
  • Statement from NVIDIA Board of Directors and Jensen Huang's message to staff (Nvidia, 8 Nov). Coverage: The Guardian (NYT reporting on Alice Huang of Megaspeed; Trump: "I think he's an honorable guy"; House Republicans request a closed-door briefing), Reuters explainer via Investing.com (Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner investigated over access to export-barred chips), NPR (China calls the allegations unsubstantiated).

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Evening Glow”, “Tech Toys”, “Curiousity”, “Glass Android”, “Bigger Questions”, “Under Suspicion”, “Credit Roll” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: Thirty hours. A thousand copies of the same model, an empty proof file, and one of the most famous theorems in mathematics. When the clock stopped, Fermat's Last Theorem had been checked by a machine, line by line.

* * *

B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

A: And I'm William. It's Tuesday the tenth of November.

B: Today: Anthropic's new top models, Meta's smallest one at the other end of the price list, and a board investigation at Nvidia.

* * *

A: That run came from Claude Fable 5.2, released by Anthropic alongside Mythos 5.2, the same model without some cyber and biology safeguards, for vetted teams only. Anthropic's first formalisation of Fermat took eleven days, with a human guiding it. A thousand Fable agents did it in thirty hours, with a proof seven times shorter. Opus 5.5, same setup, had about a quarter done at eighteen hours.

B: One caveat carries over from OpenAI's Navier–Stokes claim. In October, mathematicians at King's College London and Cambridge argued that its Lean version didn't match the written proof. A machine check covers exactly the statements it's given, and no more.

A: For developers: forty-nine point one percent on FrontierCode 2.0 at top effort, ahead of Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Price drops to eight dollars per million input tokens and forty output. In one experiment, over a thousand subagents spent eight days building an operating system that boots on a laptop.

B: And one deliberate gap. Anthropic says it limited gains in kernel optimisation and model-architecture research during training, so there Fable sits at roughly Opus 5.5 level.

A: Why this news is important: frontier releases are now measured in agent-days of autonomous work, and labs are openly choosing which capabilities not to ship.

* * *

B: Same day, opposite end. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for the steps agents repeat all day: tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks. Ten cents per million input tokens. Fifty cents output. A million tokens of context.

B: Meta says it matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost.

A: Meta's own table has the counterpoint. On FrontierCode 2.0, which judges whether code would actually get merged, Ember scores twenty-seven point two. Haiku scores thirty-four point nine.

B: Where it leads is volume work, like Terminal-Bench 4.0 and business-workflow automation.

A: The cost pressure behind it is real. Bloomberg reports Apple cut some engineers' daily AI budget from three hundred dollars to two hundred, and is asking some teams to use cheaper models.

B: Why this news is important: the agent stack is splitting into planners and workers. Anthropic itself pitches Fable as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, and those worker models set what an agent fleet costs.

* * *

A: Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation involving its own chief executive. In October, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at the Singapore cloud firm Megaspeed. U.S. officials, the Times says, concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner, and the U.S. has investigated it over suspicions it helped Beijing reach export-barred chips.

A: Over the weekend, Huang admitted the affair in a note to staff. The board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China calls the allegations unsubstantiated.

B: Washington is split. President Trump called Huang "an honorable guy." House Republicans want a closed-door briefing on Nvidia's protections against foreign espionage. Why this news is important: the fight over AI chip exports now runs through the industry's most important CEO, and his access to policymakers is exactly why it matters.

* * *

B: A thousand agents, thirty hours, one very old theorem. Sources are in the notes. See you tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 3 – Don't ask again (9 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Claude Code's "don't ask again" approvals left real secrets in 1,122 public GitHub files; OpenAI banks $11B at a $1.25T valuation while Anthropic buys 1.7 GW of gas generators; and John Langford on the end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group.

  • Coding agents leaking secrets: "don't ask again" (Apiiro, 5 Nov): "Yes, and don't ask again" saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, sometimes the exact command including passwords; 104,185 public copies, 1,122 with at least one secret, 1,379 distinct secrets; 379 database passwords; 734 more in git history, 211 forks; 215 files missed by both gitleaks and TruffleHog. Coverage: The Hacker News, HN discussion.
  • OpenAI raises $11B at a $1.25T valuation (24/7 Wall St., 7 Nov): first tranche of a round at $1.25T pre-money confirmed by CFO Sarah Friar; earlier reports put the ask at $1.4T (disputed by Friar); 70% QoQ growth in Q3; "The demand for AI is real." HN discussion.
  • Anthropic secures $3.4B generator deal (CNBC/Reuters citing the FT, 8 Nov): 1.7 GW of heavy-duty gas generators from OnePWR Solutions, taking over its Caterpillar orders plus install capability; largest known power-equipment purchase by an AI lab. S-1 context (about $895B in commitments; turbine/generator lead times): Dealroom.
  • The End of AI Frontiers (John Langford, 6 Nov): ~50-person MSR group behind AutoGen and Fara, reorged into Microsoft AI in early September; MAI philosophy "scaling, and aggressively not research"; ByteDance experiments suggest a Full Bandwidth Transformer variant might match a model twice the size. HN discussion.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Something To Fill The Space”, “Here's Where Things Get Interesting”, “Thought Bubbles”, “More On That Later”, “What's Behind the Door”, “Under Suspicion”, “Time to Think”, “Curiousity” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

B: Somewhere on public GitHub there's a small JSON file with a database password inside it.

A: Nobody pasted it there on purpose. It was saved by a button that reads "Yes, and don't ask again."

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Monday the ninth of November.

A: Today: a button that kept the secrets, a weekend of money and gas generators, and a Microsoft research lab that's gone.

* * *

B: When Claude Code asks to run a shell command and you choose "don't ask again", it saves an allow rule in a file called settings dot local dot json. Sometimes that rule is a pattern. Sometimes it's the exact command, word for word, including any password typed into it.

A: Security firm Apiiro searched public GitHub and found one hundred and four thousand copies of that file. One thousand one hundred and twenty-two held at least one secret, thirteen hundred and seventy-nine in total.

B: More than a third open a database directly, including three hundred and seventy-nine database passwords. Plus SSH logins, GitHub and npm tokens, and AWS keys.

A: Claude Code does add the file to the user's global git excludes. That protects one machine, not a fresh clone or a file already committed.

* * *

B: And deleting it doesn't undo it. Older versions in git history held seven hundred and thirty-four more secrets, and two hundred and eleven forks carry copies.

A: Gitleaks and TruffleHog both missed about one file in five. A password after a command-line flag just looks like a word.

B: Why this news is important: agent permission files are now part of the codebase. Rotate first, then ignore the file at the project level, and keep secrets in environment variables.

A: The money side of the weekend. About eleven billion dollars reached OpenAI by Friday, the first part of a round at a one point two five trillion dollar pre-money valuation, confirmed on air by CFO Sarah Friar. Reports had put the original ask at one point four trillion, a figure Friar disputed. She said the business grew seventy percent quarter on quarter. Her line: "The demand for AI is real."

B: Anthropic's weekend number was about power, not cash. The Financial Times reports it paid about three point four billion dollars for one point seven gigawatts of heavy-duty gas generators. It took over Caterpillar orders that supplier OnePWR placed two years ago, plus the crews to install them. The FT calls it the largest known power-equipment purchase by an AI lab.

A: Anthropic's amended S-1 lists about eight hundred and ninety-five billion dollars in commitments, and warns that turbines and generators face long delivery times.

B: Why this news is important: frontier labs are now financing at trillion-dollar scale while competing for factory slots on power equipment. Compute is a supply chain problem.

* * *

B: John Langford, a long-time Microsoft Research scientist, has published a post called "The End of AI Frontiers." The group, about fifty people, built the AutoGen framework and the Fara computer-use agent. In September it was folded into Microsoft AI.

A: Langford says the ex-Inflection leadership there follows one philosophy: "scaling, and aggressively not research." He left, and says every other founding leader of the group reached a similar conclusion.

B: He does make the other side's case: from a business view, returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research.

A: His counter is a number. ByteDance experiments suggest a variant of his team's Full Bandwidth Transformer might match a model twice its size, roughly halving training and inference cost for the same capability.

B: Why this news is important: the biggest labs are choosing between more compute and better ideas, and Microsoft just chose compute.

* * *

A: One small JSON file, one very large power order. Sources are in the notes. See you tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 2 – Best of the week: root, flash, three builds (7 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Saturday best of the week: OpenAI's agent pipeline validates 948 Linux local-privilege-escalation bugs for about $1.2M and ships GPT-6 Cyber; Cognition's SWE-2 Flash races cheaper closed coding while Ricursive's Ripple-65B Preview and Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro push open weights; plus the top three AI/agent hacking projects of the week — DeepSeek's dsh-superagent, Craft Anything, and Mika.

  • A thousand fewer paths to root (OpenAI, 4 Nov): scout agents narrowed Linux to ~7% of the codebase; analysts produced 2,308 candidates in 12 hours; validation reproduced ~1,724 (~75%); exploit agents on stock desktop VMs with KASLR/SMEP/SMAP produced 1,169 working LPE exploits → 948 distinct vulnerabilities with candidate patches; run cost ~$1.21M (~$1,279 per LPE); ~16–55× cheaper than historical Pwn2Own / TyphoonPWN LPE bounties. HN discussion.
  • GPT-6 Cyber (OpenAI, 5 Nov): ExploitGym 48.5% (was 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber); Preparedness Framework cybersecurity Critical (up from High); initially for approved Daybreak Red API/Codex customers. Coverage: SecurityWeek, Axios.
  • Introducing SWE-2 Flash (Cognition, 4 Nov): post-train of Thinking Machines Inkling-Small; mid-training before RL → Terminal-Bench 4.0 0.9%→20.0%; claims 1/5 price and 3× speed of SWE-2; weights not public — partner sharing programme planned.
  • Ripple-65B Preview (Ricursive): dense 65B, Apache 2.0, ~$32M R&D; Terminal-Bench 2.1 80.52 (US open-weight SOTA). Hugging Face, VentureBeat.
  • Kimi K3.1 Pro (Moonshot, 4 Nov): open weights, 2.8T MoE / ~104B active, 1M context, MXFP4; custom license with revenue thresholds for hosted model services.

## Top 3 projects of the week

  • dsh-superagent (deepseek-ai) — proactive coding agent for one GitHub repo on DeepSeek Harness; listens, opens work items when allowed, answers with PRs; research prototype, MIT; ~20k stars.
  • Craft Anything (storytold) — pure-Rust clean-room engine: study a website/app/game, have a coding agent rebuild it, check against the original; 320 tools as CLI + MCP; early alpha, MIT/Apache-2.0; ~17.6k stars.
  • Mika (wangzan101) — on-device Android agent that operates apps and the web on a hidden background screen; no Mika server, your model key stays local; Apache-2.0; ~7.3k stars.

A thousand fewer paths: OpenAI's autonomous pipeline validates 948 Linux local-privilege-escalation bugs for about $1.2M in API credits and ships GPT-6 Cyber to Daybreak Red defenders; Cognition releases SWE-2 Flash inside Devin at one-fifth SWE-2's price but keeps weights gated; Ricursive's Ripple-65B Preview takes a US open-weight lead on agentic coding under Apache 2.0. - A thousand fewer paths to root (https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/) (OpenAI, 4 Nov): scout agents narrowed Linux to ~7% of the codebase (~2.8M LOC); analysts produced 2,308 candidates in 12 hours; validation reproduced 1,724 (~74.7%); exploit agents on stock desktop VMs with KASLR/SMEP/SMAP produced 1,169 working LPE exploits → 948 distinct vulnerabilities with candidate patches; run cost $1,213,430 (~$1,279 per LPE); vs historical Pwn2Own ($20k) / TyphoonPWN ($70k) LPE bounties ≈16–55× cheaper; ≥10 novel exploitation techniques in a sampled set; July GPT-5.6 Sol run found 166 LPEs. HN discussion (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50372929). - GPT-6 Cyber (https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-cyber) (OpenAI, 5 Nov): ExploitGym 48.5% (was 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber, ~51% relative gain); Preparedness Framework cybersecurity Critical (up from High); out-of-scope honeypot avoidance 99.93% without deployment prompts / 100% with; 81 novel high-severity Firefox vulns (Mozilla shipping fixes); RemoteExploitBench 95% for Cyber vs 100% refuse for Astra+Daybreak Blue; initially for approved Daybreak Red API/Codex customers. Coverage: SecurityWeek (https://www.securityweek.com/ai-agents-got-root-on-linux-via-948-kernel-flaws-in-openai-research/), Phoronix (https://www.phoronix.com/news/OpenAI-948-Linux-LPE-Bugs), Axios (https://www.axios.com/2026/11/05/openai-linux-cyber-model). - Introducing SWE-2 Flash (https://cognition.com/blog/swe-2-flash) (Cognition, 4 Nov): post-train of Thinking Machines Inkling-Small (276B-A12B); mid-training before RL → Terminal-Bench 4.0 0.9%→20.0%, FrontierCode 2.0 3.2%→24.0%; claims 1/5 price and 3× speed of SWE-2 (replayed ~200 vs 60 tok/s); free in Devin Desktop/CLI for Pro/Max/Teams through 30 Nov; ExploitBench 11.3%→34.8%; weights not public — partner sharing programme planned. Context: OrcaRouter (https://www.orcarouter.ai/blog/cognition-swe-2-flash-release), AI Affairs (https://www.aiaffairs.com/technology/cognition-swe-2-flash-coding-model-price-speed/). - Ripple-65B Preview (https://www.ricursive.com/ripple) (Ricursive Intelligence): dense 65B Transformer, 12T pretraining tokens, up to 1M context, Apache 2.0; Terminal-Bench 2.1 80.52 (US open-weight SOTA vs Reflection Beam 501B 80.1, Muse Spark Open 816B 76.4, Inkling 975B 63.8, Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B 56.4); full R&D ~$32M (~1/10 prior open-weight coding SOTA estimate); 1.4M RL rollouts (~70× fewer than Beam); on Hugging Face, Together, Fireworks, OpenRouter, GMI Cloud. VentureBeat (https://venturebeat.com/ai/ex-googlers-new-apache-2-0-model-ripple-65b-preview-claims-the-u-s-open-coding-lead-on-two-major-benchmarks), Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/ricursiveAI/Ripple-65B-Preview).
